newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. drug agency official removed for misconduct.
newsitem.headline: U.N. drug agency official removed for misconduct.

text.p: A U.N. drug control programme employee, dogged by scandal in West Africa, has been removed from his post and will not have his contract renewed, the United Nations said on Thursday.

The staff member, Cheickh Mohamed Tidyane Bangoura of Guinea, has been accused by colleagues of sexual harassment, financial improprieties and nepotism. He was based in the Ivory Coast in 1993 and in Kenya in 1995.

Spokesman Fred Eckhard said Secretary-General Kofi Annan had consulted with the head of the Vienna-based drug control programme, Giorgia Giacomelli, about Bangoura, who he said was accused of "mismanagement and misconduct."
Giacomelli had placed Bangoura "on administrative leave and his contract, which expires at the end of the month, will not be renewed," Eckhard said.

Asked why this did not occur earlier, he said, "That is a valid question," adding that people should not be railroaded out of the U.N. system but that charges should be investigated and action taken "fairly and swiftly."

In answer to questions, he admitted the case had not come to the attention of Annan, who took office on Jan. 1, until a Washington Post investigation was published on Sunday. But other U.N. officials said Bangoura had been told months ago his contract would not be renewed.

Several creditors in the Ivory Coast say he failed to pay rent and other debts, which U.N. officials say have now been settled. He also was reported to have failed to account for thousands of dollars in U.N. funds.

The Washington Post said an internal U.N. investigation found merit in a former employee's accusation that Bangoura had sexually harassed her, although the finding was not adopted by higher U.N officials.

The newspaper said he had eluded punishment in part by invoking close ties to then-Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali, a friend of Bangoura's late father-in-law. Bangoura has called this nonsense.

Bangoura joined the U.N. drug control programme in 1992 and worked for Liselotte Waldheim-Natural, the daughter-in-law of former U.N. Secretary-General Kurt Waldheim. He became acting regional director of the U.N. drug programme, based in the Ivory Coast, in 1993, allegedly firing several workers and hiring friends and relatives.
In response to complaints from the Ivory Coast, he was moved to Kenya and the regional West African drug office was relocated to Senegal, further angering Ivorian officials.
